qs.q: A 29-year-old woman who had a term delivery six months ago presents with irregular vaginal bleeding and dyspnoea. Chest radiography reveals multiple well-defined round opacities known as cannonball metastases in both lung fields. Biopsy of a uterine lesion confirms choriocarcinoma. What is the defining histological feature of this malignancy?
o: Triploid cells with prominent stromal foetal blood vessels
Absence of chorionic villi with malignant cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast
Nested clusters of intermediate trophoblasts invading the myometrium
Presence of hyperplastic hydropic villi and trophoblasts
qs.e: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant gestational trophoblastic tumour characterised by the complete absence of chorionic villi, composed instead of abnormal cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts. Hydropic villi are found in hydatidiform moles rather than choriocarcinoma.

qs.q: A 25-year-old man is diagnosed with a pure choriocarcinoma of the testis. Laboratory evaluation is expected to consistently show an elevation in which of the following markers?
o: Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)
Prostate‑specific antigen (PSA)
Alpha‑fetoprotein (AFP)
Acid phosphatase (AP)
qs.e: Choriocarcinoma is always associated with elevated hCG because it contains syncytiotrophoblastic cells. AFP elevation indicates a yolk sac tumor component instead.
qs.s: Penile & Testicular Pathologies: Hypospadias, Tumors, Torsion – Male: MCQs

qs.q: What percentage of complete hydatidiform moles progress to give rise to choriocarcinoma?
o: Between 20 and 30%
Around 10 to 15%
Approximately 2 to 3%
Less than 1%
qs.e: 80–90% of moles resolve after curettage. 10% of complete moles are invasive, but only 2–3% give rise to choriocarcinoma.

qs.q: Gestational choriocarcinoma differs histologically from hydatidiform mole because choriocarcinoma
o: Shows hydropic swelling of chorionic villi
Demonstrates scalloped villous margins with focal atypia
Has focal trophoblastic proliferation around normal villi
Contains no chorionic villi and is composed of anaplastic trophoblasts
qs.e: Choriocarcinoma contains no chorionic villi. It is composed entirely of anaplastic cytotrophoblasts and syncytiotrophoblasts invading the myometrium and vessels.

qs.q: Why does gestational choriocarcinoma respond better to chemotherapy than gonadal choriocarcinoma?
o: Gestational tumours have lower mitotic activity overall
Paternal antigens trigger a maternal immune response aiding clearance
Gestational tumours lack TP53 mutations unlike gonadal tumours
Gestational tumours are always confined to the uterus at diagnosis
qs.e: Placental choriocarcinoma carries paternal antigens absent in gonadal tumours. A maternal immune response against these foreign antigens acts as an adjunct to chemotherapy.

es.q: Discuss the spectrum of gestational trophoblastic disease, focusing on the pathology, clinical features, diagnostic workup, management, surveillance, and specific characteristics of choriocarcinoma and gestational trophoblastic neoplasia.
es.m:
- **Definition and Spectrum**: GTD is abnormal proliferation of trophoblast, spanning benign complete and partial hydatidiform moles, invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour.
- **Gestational Trophoblastic Neoplasia (GTN)**: Invasive mole, choriocarcinoma, placental site trophoblastic tumour, and epithelioid trophoblastic tumour form GTN and are very chemosensitive.
- **Complete Mole Features**: Karyotype is 46,XX (all paternal), no foetus, all villi swollen, very high hCG, and 15-20% malignant potential for persistent disease.
- **Partial Mole Features**: Triploid (69,XXY) with one maternal and two paternal sets, foetal tissue

ai.title: Choriocarcinoma
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A malignant trophoblastic tumour lacking villi, usually follows a mole or pregnancy loss. It metastasises early via blood, most often to lungs, brain and liver.

sections.p: Choriocarcinoma is a highly malignant tumour of cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast without villi. It is a form of gestational trophoblastic disease (GTD).
b: Occurs after mole (50%), miscarriage or term pregnancy

t.b: Is the tumour marker; a plateau or rise after evacuation suggests persistent disease
Shows uterine mass; useful when hCG is rising but imaging is available
Detects pulmonary cannonball metastases; CT preferred if available

sections.p: The FIGO staging system (2000) is used: Stage I confined to uterus; Stage II pelvic extension; Stage III lung metastases; Stage IV brain, liver or other sites. Prognosis worsens with higher stage and high hCG (>100,000 IU/L).
b: Stage I – good response to single‑agent methotrexate

sections.p: The most common antecedent is a hydatidiform mole, followed by miscarriage or term pregnancy. In low‑resource settings, incomplete evacuation of a mole or retained products can precipitate choriocarcinoma.

t.b: Immunosuppression may delay diagnosis but not cause choriocarcinoma

sections.p: Patients present with abnormal uterine bleeding, pelvic pain, and sometimes systemic symptoms from metastases. Pulmonary metastases give cough, haemoptysis; brain metastases give seizures or focal deficits.
b: Persistent or rising hCG after evacuation

sections.p: Work‑up focuses on confirming GTD and staging. In low‑resource settings, basic labs and imaging may be limited; prioritize hCG and chest X‑ray.
b: If CT unavailable, use plain chest X‑ray

t.b: Baseline and serial monitoring; a plateau or rise indicates persistent disease
Detects pulmonary metastases; absence of lesions does not rule out micrometastasis
If seizures or focal signs; otherwise CT if available

sections.p: Rapidly rising hCG, haemoptysis, seizures, or severe pelvic pain are urgent signs of metastatic spread or tumour lysis. Complications include pulmonary embolism, intracranial haemorrhage and severe anaemia.

Treat the underlying GTD first: evacuate the uterus if not already done. Chemotherapy is the mainstay; methotrexate or EMA‑CO regimen depending on risk. Supportive care includes transfusion and monitoring for tumour lysis.

t.b: Chosen for low‑risk disease; avoid if renal impairment or folate deficiency
Used for high‑risk disease; includes etoposide, methotrexate, actinomycin D, cyclophosphamide, vincristine

sections.p: Serial hCG until undetectable for 3 months. Educate patients on early reporting of bleeding. Prevention focuses on prompt evacuation of molar pregnancies and close follow‑up.
b: Monthly hCG for 6 months after treatment

t.b: Early bleeding should prompt immediate clinic visit

sections.p: Ectopic pregnancy, retained products, and other GTDs such as invasive mole can mimic choriocarcinoma clinically but differ in hCG kinetics and histology.
b: Ectopic pregnancy – hCG rises but plateaus earlier

t.b: Choriocarcinoma shows sheets of trophoblast without villi

sections.p: Low hCG levels can occur in early disease; normal chest X‑ray may miss micrometastases. A single normal hCG does not exclude persistent disease.
b: Plateauing hCG – indicates need for further imaging

t.b: May be normal in early pulmonary micrometastasis

faq.q: What is the most important marker for choriocarcinoma?
faq.a: Serial serum β‑hCG; a plateau or rise after evacuation signals persistent disease.

faq.q: Why is methotrexate used in low‑risk cases?
faq.a: It is effective, inexpensive, and has a favourable toxicity profile in low‑resource settings.

faq.q: Can choriocarcinoma occur after a term pregnancy?
faq.a: Yes, although rare; it usually follows a molar pregnancy or miscarriage.

exam: What is the first investigation you would order in a patient with post‑evacuation bleeding and a rising hCG? — Serial β‑hCG; a plateau or rise indicates persistent disease.
How would you distinguish an invasive mole from choriocarcinoma on histology? — Invasive mole has villi with trophoblast invasion; choriocarcinoma lacks villi.
A patient with Stage III choriocarcinoma presents with haemoptysis. What is the next best step? — Immediate chest imaging (CT if available) and start chemotherapy.
Why is EMA‑CO preferred over single‑agent methotrexate in high‑risk disease? — It targets both trophoblast and rapidly dividing cells, improving cure rates.
What red flag would prompt urgent transfer to a higher‑level facility? — Seizure or intracranial haemorrhage from brain metastasis.
If a chest X‑ray is normal but the patient has a high hCG, what should you do? — Proceed with CT or MRI to rule out micrometastasis.
